rv.q: Her sardonic, cavorting, firecracker performance doesn’t quite conceal the weakness in her writing and the nagging sense of improbability.

Reilly has a point to make about how authentic female sexual agency can end up being commoditised and monetised by men, and the toll that sex work, of one kind or another, sometimes takes on those involved.
Just like its protagonist, the show fails to hold on to its own identity.

This is mixed in with an exposing look at influencer culture and what can be required to stay at the top of their game, often to unhealthy results. One of the most intriguing themes prominent in ROLEPLAY is the nature of currency, notably how much you value yourself, and what happens when your very values are compromised.
Roleplay is a frustrating mix of a hugely charismatic performance with a script that doesn’t quite do justice to its subject matter.
While writing this review, I found myself questioning why I was minded award a two-star rating, when it ultimately fails in the fundamental principle of having some semblance of a plot.

In other words, it’s fun to ride: intense but not too painful; it goes deep inside you without tearing you apart; and it offers some interesting reflections without coming out too thick. Its length might be problematic, though. In the end, it feels a bit too short.

cn.t: A firecracker solo performance about feminism-as-commodity can't fully overcome weak writing and thin substance in this Edinburgh transfer. Critics find it energetic and intermittently funny, but ultimately hollow.
